conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days; it helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can crop up after a baby arrives. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll take it one question at a pace that feels comfortable.

Let’s start: over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Hi Sarah. Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my husband makes a silly joke or when I see the baby’s funny faces, I do catch myself laughing. It’s not forced or anything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, that sounds right—I’ve been able to laugh. It’s not like everything’s hilarious, but I can still find things funny most of the time.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yes, I still look forward to stuff—like my morning coffee or taking the baby for a walk if it’s sunny. I don’t jump out of bed excited or anything, but little plans feel nice, not pointless.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up right after I’ve changed her, I’ll think “maybe I jostled her too much,” but I don’t keep replaying it or decide I’m a bad mom. It pops into my head and then it’s gone.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I do get a sudden “what if she stops breathing?” thought when she’s napping, but it passes pretty quickly once I peek at her on the monitor. It’s not all day—just little spikes that fade once I check on her.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t had that panicky feeling. A brief flutter of worry, sure, but nothing that feels like real fear or panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

A couple of times, like when she wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. and the laundry was piled up, I felt a bit swamped. It passed once she finally slept and I got an hour of rest. Mostly I feel like I’m keeping up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened. I’ve been sleeping pretty well—she gives me a four-hour stretch most nights—so I can’t blame unhappiness for lost sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

I’ve had a couple moments where I felt a little down—like when I couldn’t get her to nap and the day felt endless—but it lifts once she finally sleeps or I get a quiet minute to myself. It’s not a constant sad or miserable feeling.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried from being unhappy. I got a bit teary one afternoon when I was really tired, but it was more exhaustion than sadness, and it stopped once I rested.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. That idea hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 7: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)–style interview, 0–1 weeks postpartum.

Symptoms endorsed:
- Transient low mood (< day-long) tied to infant sleep difficulties  
- Momentary “what-if” catastrophic thoughts about infant safety, resolves with reassurance check  
- Occasional feeling “swamped” under high load, relieved by brief rest

Symptoms denied:
- Persistent anhedonia, pervasive guilt, crying spells, mood-related insomnia, panic attacks, self-harm ideation

Pattern: Brief, situation-specific distress without sustained depressive or anxiety symptoms; no functional impairment or safety concerns.

Screening significance:  
• Current profile below conventional cut-off for major postpartum depression or generalized anxiety; no red-flag items (self-harm, hopelessness, inability to bond).  
• Continue routine observation; educate on normative postpartum emotional lability; return if distress worsens, persists >2 weeks, or safety thoughts emerge.

Risk level at present: Low.
